title: Outage: orders stuck after yesterday's DNS server retirement

lines.text: 13:40 alert: order-sync has failed every run since 13:00; 140 orders queued for the partner, cutoff for same-day shipping 14:30
Change log, yesterday: 'retired DNS server 10.0.5.53; DHCP scope now hands out 10.0.5.2'
NetworkManager reactivated eth0 after a link flap and rewrote /etc/resolv.conf from the connection profile
14:30: same-day cutoff passed with orders still queued
14:30: every order reached the partner before the cutoff

nodes.kind: Takes orders until 14:30 for same-day shipping

objective: Diagnosing network issues: ip, ping, traceroute, ss, DNS resolution

sources.cite: CompTIA Linux+ (V8), exam XK0-006, launched 2025-07-15: System management 23%, Services and user management 20%, Security 18%, Automation, orchestration, and scripting 17%, Troubleshooting 22%
sources.note: Read through a summarizing fetch on 2026-11-16. The page lists the five domains and weights above; Troubleshooting covers diagnosing problems across the system. The objectives PDF was not opened; the course objective title is the course seed's.

Read through a summarizing fetch on 2026-11-16. Relevant text: dns=default, 'NetworkManager will update /etc/resolv.conf to reflect the nameservers provided by currently active connections'; rc-manager is 'about how NetworkManager writes to /etc/resolv.conf, if at all', and with a regular file NetworkManager writes it directly. That a hand edit is replaced the next time the connection is reactivated is the author's reading of that behavior.

Fictional hosts and addresses: the private range 10.0.5.0/24, the documentation range 203.0.113.0/24 (IETF RFC 5737) and the reserved .example names (IETF RFC 2606). Command output is an authored rendering of ip, ping, traceroute, ss, dig and nmcli output, shortened.

brief.situation: You are the Linux administrator for Brackett Foods, a fictional producer. At 13:40 monitoring reports that order-sync on app01 has failed every run since 13:00. It sends orders to a partner's API every 5 minutes; orders received by 14:30 ship the same day.
handover: Yesterday the network team retired the DNS server 10.0.5.53; DHCP now hands out 10.0.5.2.
app01 is a RHEL-family server whose network is managed by NetworkManager.
howItWorks: The terminal shows each command's output; the diagram shows app01, its gateway, both DNS servers and the partner.
Each command takes a minute; the clock moves only when you act or wait.
When you close the outage, you write the record and explain your reasoning.

source.note: The partner's same-day cutoff is 14:30, 50 minutes after the 13:40 alert.
order-sync runs every 5 minutes and sends everything queued when it can resolve the partner's name.

How many minutes each command or task takes, and when the fictional problem spreads, are teaching simplifications for exam practice, not measured values. A brief link flap at 14:10 makes NetworkManager reactivate eth0 and rewrite /etc/resolv.conf from the connection profile.

writeup.question: For the record: how you narrowed it down layer by layer, why your fix lasts, and how you checked it.

parts.label: Narrowing
parts.criteria: Shows the link, address, route and path are fine (ip, ping to the gateway and the partner's address, traceroute) and that name resolution fails (dig times out to 10.0.5.53).
parts.modelAnswer: ip showed eth0 up with its address and a default route; the gateway and 203.0.113.10 answered pings and traceroute reached the partner, so the path was fine. dig timed out against 10.0.5.53, the server retired yesterday; ss showed order-sync never connecting.

parts.label: Lasting fix
parts.criteria: Fixes the NetworkManager profile (not resolv.conf by hand, which NetworkManager rewrites; not /etc/hosts, which fixes one name) and reactivates it.
parts.modelAnswer: nmcli showed the profile pinned 10.0.5.53 and ignored DHCP's server; I set ipv4.dns 10.0.5.2 and brought the connection up, so resolv.conf is generated correctly and survives a reactivation.

parts.label: Verified
parts.criteria: Checks resolution and the service's next run, and that the queue empties before the cutoff.
parts.modelAnswer: getent resolved the partner and order-sync's log showed it sending; the queue was empty before 14:30.

expertPath.text: ip -br addr and ip route; ping the gateway and 203.0.113.10: the path is fine.
dig times out to 10.0.5.53; nmcli shows the profile pins the retired server and ignores DHCP's.
nmcli connection modify eth0 ipv4.dns 10.0.5.2, connection up; getent and the order-sync log; the queue empties on the next run.

restored.headline: Good: layer by layer, fixed at the source
restored.body: Ping by address and traceroute ruled out the path, dig showed lookups timing out against the retired server, and nmcli showed why. Fixing the profile makes NetworkManager write the right resolver every time.

restoredGaps.headline: Working, with gaps
restoredGaps.body: Orders moved, but the criteria show the fragile fix (a hand-edited resolv.conf or a hosts entry), the skipped check, or the reboot.

cutoffMissed.headline: The cutoff passed
cutoffMissed.body: The partner answered by address from the first minutes; only name resolution was broken. A hand edit of resolv.conf is undone the next time NetworkManager reactivates the connection.

stillBroken.headline: Still broken
stillBroken.body: app01 cannot resolve names. The connection profile still points at the retired DNS server.

time_up.headline: Time up
time_up.body: No record was written before the run's hard limit.

scoring.modelReasoning: Work up the stack: ip -br addr shows eth0 up with its address, ip route a default route, and the gateway and the partner's address answer pings (traceroute reaches it), so the network path is fine. dig api.partner.example times out against 10.0.5.53, the DNS server retired yesterday, and ss shows order-sync never connecting. nmcli shows the eth0 profile pins 10.0.5.53 with ignore-auto-dns, and NetworkManager writes resolv.conf from the profile, so fix the profile (ipv4.dns 10.0.5.2) and reactivate it. A hand edit of resolv.conf works until NetworkManager rewrites it; an /etc/hosts entry fixes one name and hard-codes an address. Verify with getent and the service log; the queue empties on the next run, before 14:30.
